narrative:
The model determined that you have an 86% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score had by far the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. At 24, it sits well below the average of 37 among students who were accepted, signaling that the model saw this as a major obstacle to passing the bar. Your third-year grades in law school came next in importance and also worked against you. Placing in the 3rd decile compared to an average of nearly 6th decile among accepted students, this performance further increased the predicted risk of failure. Finally, your undergraduate GPA of 2.40, noticeably lower than the 3.23 average of accepted applicants, added additional weight toward a negative outcome.

None of these factors pulled the prediction in a favorable direction. Together they created a clear picture for the model that the likelihood of passing the bar was low.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retake the LSAT and aim for a substantially higher score, while also working to raise your academic performance in law school. Improving these two elements would most effectively change future predictions in your favor.
